newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition loses legal battle over elections.
newsitem.headline: Opposition loses legal battle over elections.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties lost their legal battle for control of Belgrade on Tuesday when the Yugoslav federal supreme court refused to hear their allegations of election fraud by the ruling socialists.
More than 100,000 opposition supporters demonstrated in Belgrade for a 23rd day as the city election commission said the court decided it was not competent to rule on the conflict.

Radomir Lazarevic said "all legal remedies were exhausted" by the decision which handed the socialists a majority on the city council after opposition candidates were disqualified for unspecified "irregularities" in the November 17 election.

The Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition boycotted the federal parliament, vowing to stay away until Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic admitted he cheated them of victory in Belgrade and 14 other towns.

The socialists, determined to preserve the total power they have wielded for 50 years, used the courts to overturn the result, prompting the wave of street demonstrations demanding Milosevic's ouster.
The parliament session was the first since the socialists and their allies came within reach of a two-thirds majority in federal elections on November 3.
Although the opposition did not contest the legitimacy of the federal vote, Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic said:
"Zajedno's 22 deputies will boycott all sessions of the federal parliament until the results of the (municipal) elections are recognised."
The federal election results gave the Milosevic and his Montenegrin allies 84 of the 138 seats, just eight short of a two thirds majority which would allow him to change the constitution.
Political sources said Milosevic would not find it hard to muster the votes he needed among the smaller parties to force through constitutional change to keep him in power.
His term as Serbian president expires next year and there has been speculation he could become federal president after turning into an executive post modelled on France's powerful presidency.
The running conflict over the municipal election has upset this scenario, severely denting Milosevic's electoral credibility ahead of Serbian republic elections which must be held next year.
The U.S. and other Western governments have supported the opposition, backing their demands for socialist recognition of Zajedno's win with threats of reprisals.
The United States and NATO issued separate condemnations of Milosevic on Tuesday and the alliance praised the opposition for ensuring that its demonstrations were peaceful.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, in Brussels for a meeting of NATO foreign ministers, warned that if Milosevic wanted to "rule Serbia as an unreformed dictatorship, it will only increase his isolation and the suffering of his people."
The remark was read as a clear hint that Washington would back the re-imposition of U.N. sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia for 3-1/2 years during the war in Bosnia.
The Serbian economy is still in ruins from the last round of sanctions which mothballed industries that Milosevic has no money to revive.
But the case for sanctions is far from clearcut and Zajedno has been signalling to the West that it would oppose them.
Political sources described sanctions as a blunt instrument which would take time to have any effect and would increase the hardship of ordinary Serbs.

Milosevic's state-controlled media would almost certainly portray them as a further act of Western persecution of Serbia, a claim that would find an echo among the "silent majority" who have no source of information other than Serbian television.

Independent economist Zoran Popov told Reuters on Tuesday that Milosevic could survive for a year or two with a siege economy, barter deals with Russia and China and hard currency savings still held by Serbs.
"That way, we could still manage to increase output by some seven percent next year, albeit from a very low base," he added. "This can't go on forever but for a very long time."
